title: The Clock Inside an Atom

beats.say: Right now, your head is ageing faster than your feet. Sounds crazy. But it's true.
In October twenty twenty six, scientists built a brand new kind of clock. To see why it matters, let's go back three hundred years.
Seventeen oh seven. Sailors had a big problem. To know where they were at sea, they needed to know the exact time.
Their clocks weren't good enough. One stormy night, four British warships hit rocks. More than fourteen hundred sailors died.
So a carpenter named John Harrison spent decades building a better clock. At sea for almost three months, it lost just five seconds.
That's the secret of every clock. Something inside it ticks, again and again. The steadier the tick, the better the clock.
Harrison's clock ticked with a little swinging wheel. Today, atomic clocks count the steady wobble of an atom, billions of times every second.
Your phone's map depends on them, up in satellites. Off by just a billionth of a second, and your blue dot moves thirty centimetres.
But atoms have a weakness. Their outer parts get pushed around by heat and magnets.
So in October, two teams, in Vienna and Beijing, built clocks that listen to the atom's tiny core instead. It's better protected.
It's called a nuclear clock. It's not yet better than the best atomic clocks. But it could become around ten thousand times steadier.
Remember your head and your feet? Clocks this good can feel gravity. Time runs faster the higher you go.
So yes, your head really is older than your feet. By about half a millionth of a second, over your whole life.
